verses.text: A man of the house of Levi went and took a daughter of Levi as his wife.
The woman conceived, and bore a son. When she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
When she could no longer hide him, she took a papyrus basket for him, and coated it with tar and with pitch. She put the child in it, and laid it in the reeds by the river’s bank.
His sister stood far off, to see what would be done to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter came down to bathe at the river. Her maidens walked along by the riverside. She saw the basket among the reeds, and sent her servant to get it.
She opened it, and saw the child, and behold, the baby cried. She had compassion on him, and said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
Then his sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Should I go and call a nurse for you from the Hebrew women, that she may nurse the child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.” The maiden went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child away, and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages.” The woman took the child, and nursed it.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses,  and said, “Because I drew him out of the water.”
In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers, and looked at their burdens. He saw an Egyptian striking a Hebrew, one of his brothers.
He looked this way and that way, and when he saw that there was no one, he killed the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand.
He went out the second day, and behold, two men of the Hebrews were fighting with each other. He said to him who did the wrong, “Why do you strike your fellow?”
He said, “Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?” Moses was afraid, and said, “Surely this thing is known.”
Now when Pharaoh heard this thing, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and lived in the land of Midian, and he sat down by a well.
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water, and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.
The shepherds came and drove them away; but Moses stood up and helped them, and watered their flock.
When they came to Reuel, their father, he said, “How is it that you have returned so early today?”
They said, “An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds, and moreover he drew water for us, and watered the flock.”
He said to his daughters, “Where is he? Why is it that you have left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread.”
Moses was content to dwell with the man. He gave Moses Zipporah, his daughter.
She bore a son, and he named him Gershom,  for he said, “I have lived as a foreigner in a foreign land.”
In the course of those many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel sighed because of the bondage, and they cried, and their cry came up to God because of the bondage.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
God saw the children of Israel, and God was concerned about them.

footnotes.content: A man and woman of Levi—two ordinary people, joined together in love. The Lord looks not at fame or station, but at hearts that seek Him and each other. Their quiet faithfulness would bear such fruit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A mother sees her newborn and knows he is special—not because of his looks alone, but because she sees in him a call. She risks everything to hide him three months. Grace whispers to faith: this child is Mine too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She builds him a basket of papyrus reeds, sealed with pitch and tar—the very plants of the Nile, made into a cradle-ark. What strikes me is her tenderness in the craft itself: she did not just abandon him, but placed him with care into the river's hand, trusting the Lord who made both reeds and pharaohs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sister watches from a distance—not hiding, but present and alert. She could not save him herself, but she could stay close, ready to help when the moment came. Sometimes faithfulness is simply refusing to look away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's daughter comes to the river at just the right hour, her servants walking beside her. No accident, no luck—the Lord's hand ordering events so quietly, so naturally, that we almost miss it. He was already moving to rescue.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She opens the basket and hears the cry—a Hebrew baby, enemy's child by law. Yet her heart moves toward the infant, not away. Compassion broke through even the hatred of slavery. I've seen this in her: she knew something true about him before she knew anything else.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sister speaks up quickly, with wisdom beyond her years. 'Should I go and call a nurse?' she asks—not commanding, but offering a humble suggestion. One small act of courage at just the right moment, and the Lord's plan moves forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two words—'Go.'—and the whole rescue opens wide. Sometimes the Lord works through the gentlest consent, the smallest yes. Pharaoh's daughter did not know she was saying yes to God's will, yet there she was.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mother is restored to her own son, and she is paid for it. The Lord not only saves but restores. He gives back more than was taken. What seemed lost is returned—and the mother's love is honored, not erased.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses—'drawn out of the water.' She named him a rescuer's name, a reminder that someone had mercy on him. And indeed, he would be drawn out many times, and learn to draw others out. What we name ourselves, what we remember, shapes the souls we become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses has grown up in Pharaoh's palace, yet one day he turns away from it to go out to his brothers in their suffering. His heart knows where it belongs. Not all the riches in Egypt could keep him from the truth of his people's pain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He kills the Egyptian in anger—a swift, violent moment. Even the greatest of us stumble when we try to save ourselves by our own hand. Righteousness that comes from our own strength becomes its own kind of bloodshed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The next day, Moses tries again—this time to stop two Hebrew brothers from fighting. Still burning to fix what is broken, still reaching for the role that hasn't yet been given to him. We often run ahead of God's calling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Who made you a prince and a judge over us?' the man asks, throwing Moses' own unspoken question back at him. And Moses is afraid—not of the man, but of what he has done. Fear can be a door that opens us to hear God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well. After all the palace pomp, he finds himself in exile, waiting. Yet this is where the Lord will meet him. Sometimes we must be brought low, emptied of our own plans, before we can hear His voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest of Midian has seven daughters—a detail that seems small until you remember how carefully the Lord orders family and inheritance. One of these young women will change Moses' life, teach him faith in a foreign land, mother his children.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shepherds come and drive the daughters away, and Moses stands up to help them. Notice: he does not try to be judge or prince. He simply sees the weak being wronged, and he helps. Sometimes the smallest kindness is the truest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'How is it you've come home so early?' their father asks. A small question, but it opens the way for them to speak of the stranger who helped. Reuel is paying attention to what his daughters do, what breaks in their routine.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They call Moses 'an Egyptian'—they do not know his true name or people. Yet they recognize his kindness and speak of it truthfully. Our works often speak louder and clearer than any word we could say about ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Reuel calls Moses to stay, to eat bread with them. Here is hospitality—stranger received not with suspicion, but with the warmth of the table. I think the Lord loves when we make room for the weary without asking many questions.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses dwells with Reuel and takes Zipporah as his wife. After running, after hiding, after fear—he finds rest and love in a foreign place. The Lord gives him refuge, a family, a name among strangers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gershom—'sojourner.' Moses names his son for his exile, for the truth that he is living as a stranger in a strange land. And yet, God makes even our wilderness a place of blessing. Every exile is a classroom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Many days pass. The old king dies, but Israel's bondage does not. Yet notice—the people sigh, they cry. Their groaning rises like incense. The Lord hears what no one else hears, listens when the powerful forget to listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God heard, and God remembered—not because He had forgotten, but because the moment had come. Readers today hear an echo in these words: He remembers the covenant made with Abraham long ago, and that same God remembers the promises made to us. He is not bound by time; He moves according to His faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God saw the children of Israel, and He was concerned about them. Not distant. Not disinterested. Concerned—a father's word, a mother's eye. In their deepest darkness, they were seen, known, and held in a Father's care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
